# 2 Chronicles 27 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

Jotham's reign is the shortest account of any king of Judah in Chronicles, yet it is notably free of criticism. Both Kings and Chronicles record nothing negative about Jotham personally. The Chronicler uses him to illustrate the theme that when the Davidic king "orders his ways before the LORD," blessing, prosperity, and strength follow.

---

## v. 1 — Jotham's Accession and Mother

> *"Jotham was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem sixteen years. His mother's name was Jerushah daughter of Zadok."*

- **Ellicott** notes this is "word for word as 2 Kings 15:33," only adding the name Jotham at the start. The mother's name, Jerushah daughter of Zadok, may refer to the high priest Zadok of 1 Chronicles 6:12, suggesting a priestly lineage on his mother's side. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-27.html]

- **Precept Austin** (citing Raymond Dillard) explains that Jotham's sixteen years included a ten-year co-regency during his father Uzziah's leprosy (750–740/39 B.C.), and there was also a three-to-four-year overlap with his own son Ahaz near the end, which allows for the synchronism with Jotham's "twentieth year" mentioned in 2 Kings 15:30. [preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-27-commentary]

- **Matthew Henry** (via Precept Austin) notes that 2 Kings 15:5 tells us Jotham "was over the household, judging the people of the land" during Uzziah's leprosy — a useful apprenticeship for the young prince. [preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-27-commentary]

---

## v. 2 — Jotham's Character and the People's Corruption

> *"And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, just as his father Uzziah had done. In addition, he did not enter the temple of the LORD. But the people still behaved corruptly."*

### The "right in the eyes of the LORD" evaluation

- **David Guzik (Enduring Word)** calls Jotham "another king of Judah who was generally good," standing in strong contrast to the evil of the contemporary kings of Israel. The pattern "as his father Uzziah had done" shows the great influence a father has on a son. [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-27/]

- **Thomas Constable** summarizes: "Jotham was also a good king." [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-27.html]

### "He did not enter the temple of the LORD"

- **Ellicott** explains that this is a reservation added by the Chronicler not found in Kings. The author of Kings, having never mentioned Uzziah's sacrilege (entering the temple to burn incense), had no need to make such an exception. The Chronicler, who *did* record that episode (2 Chr 26:16–21), adds this note to clarify that Jotham did not repeat his father's great sin. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-27.html]

- **Charles Spurgeon** (quoted by both Guzik and Precept Austin) said: "He regarded his father's sin rather as a beacon to warn him away from that rock on which Uzziah's life had been wrecked." And: "It is a great mercy for us, when we have seen others sin, if we use their shipwrecks as beacons for ourselves. What fascination should there be in sin?" [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-27/]

- **Thomas Constable**: "Evidently the reference to Jotham not entering the temple means that he did not inappropriately violate the holy place as his father had done (2 Chronicles 26:16)." [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-27.html]

- **Precept Austin** adds that Jotham co-reigned with his leprous father for the first ten years. "Ten years of seeing leprosy on his father's forehead convinced him he did not want to incur the same divine curse!" The phrase does not mean he never went near the temple area, only that he "assiduously stayed away from the areas that were off limits to all but the priests." [preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-27-commentary]

- **Matthew Henry**: "He did according to all that his father did well and wisely; howbeit he would not imitate him in which he did amiss … We must not imitate the best men, and those we have the greatest veneration for, any further than they did well; but, on the contrary, their falls … must be warnings to us." [preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-27-commentary]

### "But the people still behaved corruptly"

- **Ellicott** explains this paraphrases 2 Kings 15:35 ("the people still used to sacrifice and burn incense on the high places") and notes that the contemporary prophets Micah, Hosea, and Isaiah attest to deep-seated moral corruption. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-27.html]

- **The Expositor's Bible Commentary** (via Precept Austin) observes that the Chronicler usually omits the qualifying clause about high places for good kings, but here he inserts his own: "The people did yet corruptly." He probably had in view "the unmitigated wickedness of the following reign" (Ahaz) and wanted to show that Ahaz found encouragement for his idolatry, while being careful that "no shadow of blame falls upon Jotham." [preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-27-commentary]

- **Thomas Constable**: "Jotham appears to have failed to lead his people in righteousness. There was no reformation of abuses or revival during his reign, as far as we know." [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-27.html]

- **David Guzik** notes that the word "still" is important — the corruption did not begin under Jotham but continued from Uzziah's day. Payne (quoted by Guzik) says: "Below the surface prosperity that was enjoyed by both kingdoms at this time, the contemporary preaching of Hosea and Amos indicates the presence of serious moral and spiritual decay." [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-27/]

- **Matthew Henry** suggests this "perhaps reflects some blame upon him, that he was wanting in his part towards the reformation of the land. Men may be very good themselves, and yet not have courage and zeal to do what they might do towards the reforming of others." [preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-27-commentary]

- **L.M. Grant** (via Precept Austin): "Though Jotham was personally faithful to the Lord, he did not have the spiritual energy to banish the false worship from Judah." [preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-27-commentary]

---

## v. 3 — Building the Upper Gate and the Wall of Ophel

> *"Jotham rebuilt the Upper Gate of the house of the LORD, and he worked extensively on the wall at the hill of Ophel."*

- **Ellicott** clarifies: "He built" means "He it was that built" (pronoun emphatic) — he restored and beautified. "The high gate" is better rendered "the Upper Gate," meaning the northern gate of the inner or upper court (see Ezekiel 9:2). The north was considered the holy quarter (Isaiah 14:13; Psalm 48:2). Ophel was the southern slope of the Temple hill, meaning "the mound." Its wall was the line of fortifications connecting Zion with Moriah, on which Uzziah had already worked (2 Chr 26:9), securing the city against attacks from the south and east. Neither this detail nor the next three verses appear in the parallel account in Kings, indicating a good ancient source. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-27.html]

- **David Guzik** (quoting Knapp) sees profound spiritual symbolism: "He wished free access from his own house to that of the Lord. He would strengthen the link between the two houses — keep his line of communication open (to use a military figure) with the source of his supplies of strength and wisdom. This is one of the secrets of his prosperity and power." Guzik adds: "His father Uzziah misunderstood the link between the royal house and the house of God, demanding priestly authority … Many kings before him wanted no link between the royal house and the house of God. Jotham understood that he was a king and not a priest, yet he wanted a good, open link between the palace and the temple." [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-27/]

- **Pulpit Commentary Homiletics** (on BibleHub) sees a principle of working "from within outward": "First, 'he built the high gate' of the temple; that was beginning at the very centre, at 'the house of the Lord' … This is the true order. Let solicitude and activity begin at the centre — at a man's own heart and character; let them move outward — to those in the home circle … and then to those still further away." [biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/2_chronicles/27.htm]

- **Matthew Henry**: "He began with the gate of the house of the Lord, which he repaired, beautified, and raised." [preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-27-commentary]

---

## v. 4 — Building Cities, Fortresses, and Towers

> *"He also built cities in the hill country of Judah and fortresses and towers in the forests."*

- **Ellicott**: "Literally, and cities built he in the hill region of Judah. (Comp. 2 Chronicles 26:10.)" The word for "castles" is *bîrânîyôth*, a term also used in 2 Chronicles 17:12. Ellicott adds a striking note: "The contemporary prophets denounced the popular confidence in 'fenced cities' as a kind of treason against Jehovah, who was Himself the shield and fortress of His people." He cites Hosea 8:14: "Israel hath forgotten his Maker, and buildeth palaces; and Judah hath multiplied fenced cities: but I will send a fire upon his cities, and it shall devour the palaces thereof." [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-27.html]

- **David Guzik** (citing Patterson and Austel): "He also turned his attention to urban planning, constructing cities in the highlands of Judah that, together with a system of towers and fortification in the wooded areas, could serve both economic and military purposes." [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-27/]

- **Precept Austin**: "His building program shows a king devoted to strengthening the internal life of Judah rather than seeking glory abroad. By establishing cities in the hill country, Jotham encouraged settlement and stability in regions that likely had been thinly populated and vulnerable to raids." [preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-27-commentary]

- **Andrew Hill** (NIV Application Commentary, via Precept Austin) notes the Chronicler applauds Jotham on three fronts: "his building program, his military success, and his consolidation of political power (2 Chr 27:3–6)." [preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-27-commentary]

---

## v. 5 — War with the Ammonites and Tribute

> *"Jotham waged war against the king of the Ammonites and defeated them, and that year they gave him a hundred talents of silver, ten thousand cors of wheat, and ten thousand cors of barley. They paid him the same in the second and third years."*

- **Ellicott** explains: "'He also,' like his father, 'fought with the king of the sons of Ammon.' They no doubt had refused the tribute imposed on them by Uzziah; but Jotham quelled their resistance, and they paid him a fixed contribution for three successive years." A kor was perhaps equivalent to a quarter (a dry measure). Ellicott suggests: "After three annual payments, the tribute was again suspended, perhaps because the Ammonites took advantage of the outbreak of the Syro-Ephraite war, which took place towards the end of the reign (2 Kings 15:37)." [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-27.html]

- **David Guzik** (citing Selman): "The tribute was substantial, something over three tons of silver and approximately ten thousand donkey loads of barley." [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-27/]

- **L.M. Grant** (via Precept Austin) offers a typological reading: "The Ammonites picture the doctrine of demons, which, though not destroyed, were allowed no liberty during Jotham's reign." [preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-27-commentary]

- **Matthew Henry**: "He prevailed against the Ammonites, who had invaded Judah in Jehoshaphat's time (2 Chr 20:1). He triumphed over them, and exacted great contributions from them." [preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-27-commentary]

---

## v. 6 — The Secret of Jotham's Strength

> *"So Jotham grew powerful because he ordered his ways before the LORD his God."*

This is the theological heart of the chapter and the Chronicler's key evaluation.

### The meaning of "ordered his ways" (or "prepared his ways")

- **Ellicott**: The Hebrew means "he directed his ways" (compare Proverbs 21:29; 2 Chronicles 12:14; 20:33). "'Before' … in the chronicler's usage, 'to meet,' 'towards' Jehovah his God. (Comp. 1 Chronicles 12:17; 1 Samuel 7:3.) … Perhaps, however, 'before' simply means 'as in the sight of' Jehovah. (Comp. Genesis 17:1, 'walk before me.')" The verse is "a moral reflection of the writer on the preceding facts." [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-27.html]

- **Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary** notes the marginal reading is "established his ways" — indicating steadfastness: "He was not fickle-minded, carried about by every wind that blew, but having prepared his heart to serve the Lord, God was pleased to give him a steadiness of heart." [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-chronicles-27.html]

### Spurgeon's Sermon on This Verse

- **Charles Spurgeon** preached an entire sermon on this verse (published 1907) titled "Jotham's Peculiar Honor." He said: "This is a very singular expression which is used here concerning Jotham … it is mentioned as his peculiar honor that he 'became mighty, because he prepared his ways before the Lord his God.'" Spurgeon drew out three points: (1) Jotham resolved to do what God bade him, making God's Law the rule of his life; (2) "Jotham must have been a man of prayer. He could not have prepared his ways thus anywhere except at the Mercy Seat"; (3) Jotham was steadfast — "My heart is fixed, O God, my heart is fixed" (the marginal reading being "prepared"). Spurgeon said: "The real reason why Jotham's heart was prepared and established before God was because his heart was right with God. And how did his heart get to be right with God? Why, in the same way as yours and mine must — by being created anew!" [ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons53.xliii.html]

- Spurgeon also emphasized that Jotham became "mighty in resolve": "That man who has prepared his heart and his ways with a single eye to God's Glory, resolving only to do the right thing whatever may happen, is the man who has a right to say, 'I will,' and 'I shall.'" [ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons53.xliii.html]

### The Upper Gate as the means of preparation

- **Knapp** (quoted in Enduring Word): "That high gate between the palace and the temple was better than a Chinese wall around his kingdom. It is in communion with God that real prosperity and power is found." [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-27/]

- **G. Campbell Morgan** (quoted in Enduring Word): "While there was no definite national reform during his reign, he seems to have gone quietly forward along true lines, and his strength is attributed to the fact that he ordered his ways before Jehovah his God." [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-27/]

- **F.B. Meyer** (quoted in Enduring Word): "I do not remember ever meeting one who really walked with God who did not make orderliness one of the first principles of life … They are the habits of the soul that walks before God, and which is accustomed to think of Him as seeing in secret, and considering all our ways." [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-27/]

### Jotham's unique distinction

- **Knapp** (Enduring Word): "Jotham is the only one of all the Hebrew kings, from Saul down, against whom God has nothing bad to record. In this his character is in beautiful accord with his name, Jehovah-perfect." [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-27/]

- **Bob Utley** (Precept Austin): "It is surprising that nothing negative is said about this king. He was faithful from the first to the last. The only negative item (2 Chr. 27:2) is attributed to 'the people.' Because of this it is surprising he does not receive more attention from the Chronicler. Also note that he did not have a godly counselor, did not receive a prophetic warning and did not receive a priestly warning." [preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-27-commentary]

- **Frederick Mabie** (Expositor's Bible Commentary, via Precept Austin): "Unlike Uzziah, however, Jotham did not grow proud and challenge Yahweh's covenantal bounds regarding temple service, but instead 'walked steadfastly' (or better, 'caused his ways to be ordered') before the Lord." [preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-27-commentary]

- **Matthew Henry**: "He walked circumspectly and with much caution, contrived how to shun that which was evil and compass that which was good. He looked before him, and cast his affairs into such a posture and method as made the regular management of them the more easy … The more stedfast we are in religion the more mighty we are both for the resistance of that which is evil and for the performance of that which is good." [preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-27-commentary]

---

## v. 7 — The Rest of Jotham's Acts

> *"As for the rest of the acts of Jotham, along with all his wars and his ways, they are indeed written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah."*

- **Ellicott** observes that the Chronicler varied the phrase from 2 Kings 15:36 ("And all that he did") to "all his wars and his ways," in order "to hint at the Syro-Ephraite war, mentioned in 2 Kings 15:37." That verse says: "In those days the LORD began to send Rezin king of Aram and Pekah the son of Remaliah against Judah." [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-27.html]

- **David Guzik** (citing Dilday): "During Jotham's reign, the combined forces of King Rezin of Syria and King Pekah of Israel began their invasion of Judah, but the full impact of these military assaults was not felt until Jotham's son became king." Guzik also notes that 2 Kings 15:37 says "it was the hand of the LORD that sent these foreign rulers who troubled Judah." [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-27/]

- **Payne** (Enduring Word) suggests: "The reference to 'all' Jotham's wars suggests that prior to the Ammonite campaign, for which as king he had sole responsibility, he may have served as field commander for the alliance that was conceived by his quarantined father, Uzziah." [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-27/]

- **Matthew Henry**: "His wars and his ways, his wars abroad and his ways at home, were so glorious that they were recorded in the book of the kings of Israel, as well as of the kings of Judah." [preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-27-commentary]

---

## v. 8 — Summary Repetition of Age and Reign

> *"He was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem sixteen years."*

- **Ellicott** says this is "a word for word repetition of 2 Kings 15:33, omitting the last clause about the queen-mother." He suggests: "Perhaps in one of the chronicler's sources this notice occurred at the beginning, and in another at the end of the reign. This would account for its repetition here, after having been already stated in 2 Chronicles 27:1." [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-27.html]

- **Matthew Henry** notes: "He finished his course too soon, but finished it with honour. He had the unhappiness to die in the midst of his days; but, to balance that, the happiness not to out-live his reputation, as the last three of his predecessors did. He died when he was but forty-one years of age." [preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-27-commentary]

---

## v. 9 — Death and Succession

> *"And Jotham rested with his fathers and was buried in the City of David. And his son Ahaz reigned in his place."*

- **David Guzik**: "After the stories of the three previous kings, each of whom started well but finished poorly, it is somewhat of a relief to read of a king who did not have such a disappointing end." [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-27/]

- **Matthew Henry**: "The last words of the chapter are the most melancholy, as they inform us that Ahaz his son, whose character, in all respects, was the reverse of his, reigned in his stead. When the wealth and power with which wise men have done good devolve upon fools, that will do hurt with them, it is a lamentation, and shall be for a lamentation." [preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-27-commentary]

- **GotQuestions.org** (via Precept Austin) notes that despite Jotham's godly example and Ahaz's wickedness, "both Jotham and Ahaz are ancestors of Jesus Christ (Matthew 1:9). God is able to use all people to accomplish His good purposes." [preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-27-commentary]

---

## Denominational Distinctives and Other Views

### Where traditions differ

The account of Jotham is brief and uncontroversial, so there are relatively few points of sharp denominational disagreement. However, emphases differ:

- **Reformed / Baptist (Spurgeon, via ccel.org):** Strong emphasis on God's sovereign, supernatural work in preparing Jotham's heart: "The real reason why Jotham's heart was prepared … was because his heart was right with God. And how did his heart get to be right with God? Why, in the same way as yours and mine must — by being created anew!" This is a classic Reformed emphasis on regeneration preceding faith and obedience. [ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons53.xliii.html]

- **Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Strong emphasis on personal prayer as the mechanism of Jotham's strength, quoting Spurgeon on Jotham being "at the mercy-seat" and Knapp on "constant communion with God." The focus is on maintaining a living, experiential link with God. [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-27/]

- **Dispensational (L.M. Grant, via Precept Austin):** A typological reading where the Ammonites "picture the doctrine of demons, which, though not destroyed, were allowed no liberty during Jotham's reign." This reflects a dispensational tendency to read Old Testament narratives as patterns for spiritual warfare in the church age. [preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-27-commentary]

### What could not be found

- **Lutheran** (lcms.org, 1517.org), **Methodist/Wesleyan** (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com), **Catholic** (newadvent.org, catholic.com), **Orthodox** (oca.org), **NET Bible notes**, and **Bible Odyssey** (modern scholarship) did not return results in the available searches for specific 2 Chronicles 27 commentary.

---

## Summary of Key Themes

1. **Learning from others' failures:** Jotham saw his father's leprosy daily and used it as a warning beacon rather than repeating Uzziah's pride (v. 2).

2. **The priority of the temple:** Jotham began his building program at the house of the LORD — the Upper Gate — before expanding outward to cities, fortresses, and foreign conquest (vv. 3–5).

3. **Personal godliness without national reform:** Jotham was personally upright, but the people "still behaved corruptly." He did not lead a national revival, yet he himself remained faithful (v. 2).

4. **Strength through ordered ways before God:** The Chronicler's central theological note is that Jotham's might came from "ordering" or "preparing his ways before the LORD" — a phrase encompassing prayer, deliberate obedience, steadfastness, and living with an awareness of God's presence (v. 6).

5. **A quiet, steady reign:** Unlike his predecessors, Jotham started well and finished well, making him (along with Solomon) one of the only kings of whom Scripture records nothing negative — "Jehovah-perfect."
